title: Bigger, the best
goal: Describing and comparing — and why Mongolian "than" uses the same suffix as "from".
bekal: use adjectives correctly, including the "-ish" and "very" degrees
compare two things with the *-аас* suffix and the word *илүү*

dialogs.title: Яриа — Аль нь дээр вэ?
dialogs.intro: Budi wants to buy a winter jacket. Sarnai goes to the shop with him and they compare two options.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: The black one is nice. But the blue one looks warmer.
lines.literal: black -the nice is. but blue -the more warm probably.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: The blue one looks more expensive than the black one, you know.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Twenty thousand. But it's wool, and the quality is much better.
lines.literal: twenty thousand. but wool's, quality -the no-matter better.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: How cold is winter in Ulaanbaatar?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Very cold. It's the coldest capital in the world, you know.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Indonesia is thirty degrees, here it's minus thirty. That's a sixty-degree difference.
lines.literal: Indonesia thirty degree, here minus thirty degree. sixty degree's difference.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Terrifying! Then I'll take the warmest jacket.
lines.literal: scary! then most warm jacket-object let's-take.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Good decision. Buy a cheap jacket and you'll end up buying twice.
lines.literal: right decision. cheap jacket if-buy later two time buy.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Do I need a hat too?

lines.id: Definitely! Go out without a hat and your ears will freeze.
lines.literal: surely! hat-without if-go-out ear your freeze.

lines.id: OK, so you mean get the thickest hat?
lines.literal: OK, most thick hat-object -the take-please so say Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Exactly. Warmth matters more than looks.
lines.literal: exactly so. pretty beauty-from warm -the important.

notes: ⚠️ **Mongolian comparison uses the -аас suffix, the same one as "from".** *Харнаас үнэтэй* = "more expensive **than** the black one" (literally "from the black one, pricey"). The logic makes sense: you measure something **starting from** another point. Latin did something similar with its ablative, and English still says "different **from**".
**Илүү (more) is optional.** *Харнаас үнэтэй* and *харнаас илүү үнэтэй* mean the same. The *-аас* suffix alone already signals a comparison. People add *илүү* for emphasis.
**Хамгийн = most, and it sits right in front of the adjective.** *Хамгийн сайхан* (the nicest), *хамгийн хүйтэн* (the coldest). It's the only superlative form you need at A1.

**Нь is a tiny word meaning "its / the one" and it's used constantly.** *Хар **нь*** = "the black one" (literally: black-its); *чанар **нь*** = its quality. It turns an adjective into a noun and marks third-person possession at the same time.

**Байх at the end of a sentence means "probably, seems".** *Илүү дулаан **байх*** = it's probably warmer. ⚠️ Don't confuse it with *байх* as the dictionary form of "to be" — its position at the very end, after an adjective, gives it away.

grammars.title: Comparing two things
body: The order: **thing compared to + -аас + adjective**. The subject comes first, then the yardstick, then the quality — the reverse of English "bigger than that".
after: ⚠️ Look at the third row: *том* means "big" **and** "older". Mongolian uses one word for both, much like English "big sister" or "big brother". *Би чамаас том* in conversation almost always means age, not body size.
**To say "as … as" or "the same", use *шиг* (like) or *адилхан* (same).** *Энэ түүн **шиг** том* = this is as big as that; *хоёулаа **адилхан*** = both are the same.

grammars.title: Degrees of adjectives
body: Mongolian has five degrees, and three of them are made with an attached suffix — not with a separate word, as in English.
after: ⚠️ The suffix **-втар / -втор** makes colors "-ish": *улаан* (red) → *улаавтар* (reddish); *хөх* (blue) → *хөхөвтөр* (bluish); *шар* (yellow) → *шаравтар* (yellowish). It works exactly like English "-ish".

**Маш and их both mean "very", and you can combine them for extra emphasis:** *маш их сайхан* = really very nice. If you want just one, use *маш* — it's a bit stronger and more common in conversation.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Tell **сайн** and **сайхан** apart: *сайн* means "good" in quality and morals (*сайн хүн* — a good person), while *сайхан* means "beautiful, pleasant" (*сайхан өдөр* — a lovely day). Beginners mix them up often, and the result is funny but not fatal: *сайхан хүн* means "a good-looking person", not "a good person".

blocks.title: Adjectives go BEFORE the noun, always
items: *том ном* (big book), *шинэ гэр* (new home), *хамгийн сайхан өдөр* (the loveliest day).
⚠️ Same as English, so this one comes naturally. Just don't let other languages you know (French, Spanish) tempt you into *ном том*.
**Adjectives never change form** — not for plural, not for case. *Том ном*, *том номууд*, *том номыг*: the adjective stays *том*.
When an adjective comes after the noun, it becomes the **predicate**: *Ном том.* = "The book is big." Different position, different role — just like "a big book" versus "the book is big".

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Таалагдах* means "to be liked" and works **backwards** compared with English: the thing liked is the subject, and the person takes the *-д* suffix. *Надад энэ таалагдаж байна* is literally "to me this is pleasing". It's exactly like Spanish *me gusta*, or English "this appeals to me".
For a simpler "like", use *дуртай* (fond of): *Би цайнд дуртай* = "I like tea". The person is the subject, and the thing liked takes *-д*. This form is much easier and just as correct — use it at A1.

Notice the **-тай** suffix you already know: *салхи* (wind) → *салхитай* (windy); *цас* (snow) → *цастай* (snowy). Mongolian describes weather as something **the day has** — a lot like English "-y" in "windy" and "snowy".

blocks.title: ⚠️ Numbers you should take seriously
items: Ulaanbaatar is **the coldest capital in the world**, with a yearly average of about −1°C (30°F).
January averages **−25°C (−13°F)**, and −40°C is nothing unusual. Jakarta on the same day is about +30°C — **a seventy-degree difference.**
Summer can reach +35°C. Mongolia has the largest yearly temperature swing of any capital in the world.

That's why *хүрэм* (jacket), *малгай* (hat), *бээлий* (gloves) and *гутал* (boots) aren't accessories but survival gear. Buy them in Mongolia — what's sold there is actually made for those temperatures.
